subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Pulsars: Spinning Beacons
description: A micro-lesson that makes Pulsars: Spinning Beacons usable.

hook.text: Pulsars are neutron stars that emit beams of radiation from their poles. Each rotation produces a pulse.

buildup.text: They spin so regularly that early discoverers thought they'd found alien signals—calling them 'LGM' (Little Green Men).

discovery.text: The fastest known pulsar spins 716 times per second. Its surface moves at a quarter the speed of light.

twist.text: Pulsar timing is so precise that slight irregularities revealed the first exoplanets ever found—in 1992.

climax.text: Arrays of pulsars are being used to detect gravitational waves washing over the entire galaxy.

punchline.text: Dead stars spinning 716 times a second. Nature's most precise clocks.

quiz.question: Why were pulsars initially nicknamed 'LGM' (Little Green Men)?
options: Their incredibly regular pulses seemed like artificial alien signals
They emitted a green-colored light visible through telescopes
They were found near star systems thought to harbor aliens

details.summary: Pulsars are rapidly rotating neutron stars that emit beams of radiation from their magnetic poles. As the star spins, these beams sweep across space like lighthouse beacons. When a beam points toward Earth, we detect regular pulses — so precise that they rival atomic clocks in timekeeping accuracy.
details.whyItMatters: Pulsars are nature's most precise clocks. Their ultra-regular pulses detect gravitational waves, test general relativity, and map the interstellar medium. One pulsar system provided the first indirect evidence of gravitational waves.
takeaways: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars with radiation beams
Their pulses are so regular they rival atomic clocks
They've provided indirect evidence of gravitational waves

faq.question: How were pulsars discovered?
faq.answer: Jocelyn Bell Burnell detected the first pulsar in 1967 as a regular radio signal pulsing every 1.337 seconds. Initially dubbed 'LGM-1' (Little Green Men), it was soon recognized as a rotating neutron star. Her supervisor Antony Hewish received the Nobel Prize — controversially without her.

faq.question: What is a millisecond pulsar?
faq.answer: A neutron star spun up to hundreds of rotations per second by accreting matter from a companion star. The infalling material transfers angular momentum, accelerating the pulsar. Millisecond pulsars are the most stable natural clocks, useful for detecting gravitational waves through timing arrays.
